headline: Meta emphasizes connection, impact, and AI innovation; DEI language surged 2016–2020, then stabilized as AI became central.
identity: Meta has consistently valued openness, human connection, and making a real-world impact—themes that persist across its entire recruiting history. Altruism and inclusion language peaked around 2016–2020, with explicit DEI commitments and belonging-focused messaging. However, by 2025–2026, the careers copy has pivoted sharply: AI mentions jumped from near-zero to 44% of all content (2026), while inclusion and meritocracy language retreated significantly. DEI language did not disappear, but it is now subordinate to techno-optimism and AI capability.
fit: You might be a good fit if you are drawn to fast-paced, high-impact technical work and believe technology can solve large problems. Meta's language reaches for people excited by "big questions," willing to "move fast," and energized by building at scale—especially in AI and hardware. If you value explicit diversity commitments and belonging-centered culture, the 2016–2021 messaging was stronger; recent copy emphasizes innovation and capability over inclusion.

sections.heading: The Rise and Plateau of Altruism & Inclusion (2009–2022)
sections.body:
From 2009 to 2015, Meta's careers copy leaned heavily on social mission: "making the world more open and connected" and "building real value for the world." Altruism scores climbed steadily, peaking in 2016 (zscore 1.72) with language about "a better, more connected world for everyone."

DEI language emerged explicitly around 2013 ("be yourself") and intensified sharply in 2020, when inclusion scores hit their highest point (zscore 1.83). The 2020–2021 period featured explicit demographic language ("underrepresented communities," "women," "LGBTQ," "faith"), structural belonging initiatives (resource groups, mentorship), and repeated statements that "diversity is a must-have, not an option." This was the company's most DEI-forward moment.

By 2022, altruism and inclusion remained elevated but began to soften. The language shifted from explicit demographic categories toward vaguer aspirational framing ("diverse backgrounds," "unique perspectives"). Meritocracy language stayed steady, but the emotional intensity around belonging declined.

sections.heading: The AI Pivot (2022–2026)
sections.body:
AI mentions were virtually absent until 2019 (one mention, 4.8% prevalence). By 2022, AI appeared in 8.3% of content. Then, in 2025, AI language exploded to 44.4% of all careers copy—14 mentions of "AI" and references to "large language models," "Llama," and "Meta AI." By 2026, every single chunk of mission-brand content (11 of 11) mentioned AI.

This shift came with a measurable cost to other messaging. Inclusion scores dropped from 0.57 (2025) to 0.26 (2026)—a 54% decline. Meritocracy scores fell from 0.46 to 0.21. Performance language, which had been steady around 0.43–0.49, collapsed to 0.25. The careers copy in 2026 is almost entirely product-focused: Ray-Ban glasses, Quest headsets, Llama models, AR prototypes. Human-centered language about belonging, growth, or care is minimal.

Techno-optimism, by contrast, surged. From a zscore of 0.04 in 2023, it jumped to 1.85 (2025) and 2.70 (2026)—the highest in the entire dataset. Phrases like "mind-blowing," "breakthrough," "pushing the limits," and "next-generation" dominate the 2026 copy.

sections.heading: What Persisted and What Faded
sections.body:
Craft and performance language remained relatively stable across the period, suggesting Meta never stopped emphasizing execution and quality. Altruism dipped slightly after 2018 but stayed above baseline through 2025, only to vanish in 2026.

Wellbeing language (benefits, flexibility, care) peaked in 2016 and 2022, then declined. By 2026, it is nearly absent—the 2026 careers copy mentions product features, not employee experience.

The most striking absence is *human connection as a value for employees*. From 2009–2022, Meta repeatedly said "people are at the heart of every connection we build" and emphasized collaboration. By 2026, that language is gone. Instead, the copy focuses on what employees will build (AI, glasses, metaverse infrastructure), not how they will work together or grow.

Inclusion language did not vanish entirely—2025 still includes "diverse backgrounds," "unique insights," and "everyone has a voice." But it is now framed as instrumental ("diverse teams make better products") rather than intrinsic ("we value you for who you are"). The register shifted from belonging-culture to aspirational-vague.
